body:
The paper's two headline operating points are:

| Clean ancillas | Dirty ancillas | Toffoli cost |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 | 0 | \(\boxed{4n\pm O(1)}\) |
| 2 | \(n-2\) | \(\boxed{3n\pm O(1)}\) |

The second construction uses a dirty secondary register for carry-xor operations. The first obtains constant total workspace by splitting the target into two halves and letting each half borrow the other as dirty workspace at different stages. (pp. 1, 3, and 7; Figs. 4-5.)
summary: The principal operating points trade three clean ancillas for \(4n\) Toffolis or use \(n-2\) dirty ancillas to reach \(3n\).
title: Principal workspace/Toffoli tradeoffs

body:
Define

\[
x'=x+d+c_0
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{carry}(x,d,c_0)
=x\oplus d\oplus(x+d+c_0).
\]

The identity is

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{carry}(\sim x',d,c_0)
=\operatorname{carry}(x,d,c_0)}.
\]

Thus the carries can be recomputed from values available after the addition. They are "Z-redundant": measuring a carry qubit in the \(X\) basis frees the qubit, while a minus outcome leaves a known deferred phase-flip task. The paper calls this conversion from carry garbage into phase obligations **venting**. (Eq. 8 and Sec. 2.2, p. 3.)
summary: The carry string can be reconstructed after addition, allowing X-basis measurement to replace carry garbage with deferred phase work.
title: Carry identity used for venting

body:
The classical offset enters the circuit through its bits \(d_k\). To control the whole addition:

- replace every hardwired \(d_k=0\) by 0;
- replace every hardwired \(d_k=1\) by the outer control qubit.

The \(d_k\) values are used only to invert controls or to control bit flips. Substituting the outer control into those positions does not promote any existing operation into a higher-controlled nonlinear gate, so the paper counts **no additional workspace and no additional Toffolis**. (Sec. 2.4, p. 7; Fig. 6.)
summary: The outer control substitutes for hardwired one-bits of the classical offset, adding no nonlinear gates in the paper’s accounting.
title: Why an outer control adds no Toffolis

summary: Conditional swaps orient all four Kaliski cases into a single subtract/add, halve, and double round body.
title: Normalizing the four Kaliski cases

body:
For \(n\)-bit inputs, the classical Kaliski execution uses some \(k\) with

\[
n\leq k\leq 2n.
\]

The reversible circuit always executes \(\boxed{2n}\) scheduled rounds; only \(k\) rounds modify the EEA state. A counter records \(2n-k\), and the initial output is the pseudo-inverse

\[
x^{-1}2^{-n+k}\pmod p.
\]

The desired Montgomery inverse is

\[
x^{-1}2^n\pmod p,
\]

so the copied output needs exactly \(2n-k\) modular doublings.

The paper folds these doublings into inverse-circuit cleanup. During reversal of the \(2n\) rounds, the same round control selects either:

- uncomputing an active division round; or
- doubling the copied output for an inactive round.

These operations can run in parallel, so the variable correction is completed during cleanup without a separate correction pass or an increase in total gate count. (Sec. 4.2, p. 8.)
summary: The circuit schedules \(2n\) rounds and performs the \(2n-k\) correction doublings concurrently with reverse cleanup.
title: Fixed rounds and integrated pseudo-inverse correction

body:
**Producer/consumer fusion.** To compute \(xy+z\), the paper keeps the multiplication's auxiliary state alive, replaces Bennett's result-copy CNOT layer by the addition into \(z\), and only then reverses the multiplier. The cost becomes one multiplication plus one addition, rather than two multiplications plus one addition. Applied to squaring followed by subtraction in point addition, this saves almost half the squaring cost and depth and removes an auxiliary register. (Sec. 4.1, p. 7; Fig. 5.)

**Workspace reuse.** After modular inversion, three registers contain known values \(0\), \(1\), and \(p\). The circuit clears them with at most \(3n\) parallel X gates and reuses their qubits as the workspace for modular multiplication before completing inversion uncomputation. (Sec. 4.2, pp. 8-10; Fig. 8.)
summary: Consume a producer’s result before reversing its garbage, and reuse registers that temporarily hold known constants.
title: Producer/consumer and workspace-reuse examples

body:
Write each EEA step as a small transition matrix \(\tau_i\), with

\[
\tau_{\mathrm{total}}=\tau_m\tau_{m-1}\cdots\tau_1.
\]

- **Explicit access:** compute and store the full product \(\tau_{\mathrm{total}}\), including the coefficient arrays of the final Bézout polynomials. This is required when later logic needs the polynomial coefficients as ordinary data.

- **Implicit access:** store a compact representation of each \(\tau_i\), without multiplying the sequence into full Bézout polynomials. A consumer is rewritten to replay the transformations on an appropriate vector. The Bézout object exists as an executable transformation sequence, not as a materialized coefficient register.

Both approaches target leading-order space \(2nb+O(\log_2 n)\), but the implicit construction uses the cheaper constant-time, division-free EEA structure. (Secs. II.B.1-3, pp. 8-13.)
summary: Explicit access materializes the total Bézout matrix; implicit access keeps the EEA transition sequence executable.
title: Explicit versus implicit Bézout access

summary: Applying the EEA transition product to \([0,A]^T\) emits \(AB^{-1}\) directly without storing \(B^{-1}\).
title: Direct division without materializing \(B^{-1}\)

summary: Dialog records elementary EEA transitions, but its \(\mathrm{GF}(2^b)\) resource counts do not transfer directly to carry-based prime-field arithmetic.
title: What the Dialog encodes and transfer limitation

summary: Ghosting resets a quantum value while retaining a classical string that indexes the resulting phase; distinct labels prevent amplitude collisions.
title: Ghosting transformation and precondition

body:
The exact relation appears in two closely related forms:

- **Unghosting, Lemma 3.5:** if
  \[
  \boxed{n\leq\binom{m+s-1}{s-1}},
  \]
  a line of length \(n\) can be unghosted with at most \(s\) pebbles and \(O(mn)\) steps.

- **Pebbling, Theorem 3.6:** after the one-pebble conversion,
  \[
  \boxed{n\leq\binom{m+s-2}{s-2}+1},
  \]
  a line of length \(n\) can be pebbled with at most \(s\) pebbles and \(O(mn)\) steps.

The paper's summary table suppresses the harmless \(+1\) and presents the condition in the form \(\binom{m+s-2}{s-2}\geq n\). (pp. 3 and 10.)
summary: Binomial relations characterize the line length reachable with a bounded number of pebbles and a time parameter.
title: Binomial line-length relation

body:
The recycled qubits do not eliminate the full memory obligation. The measurement bitstring \(b\) must remain in **classical ancillary memory** from ghosting until the original value can be recomputed and the phase can be removed. Correspondingly, the paper reduces quantum memory but not total memory measured as classical bits plus qubits. (pp. 2, 5-6.)

Operationally, a ghosted register has two pieces of outstanding state:

1. a reusable standard-basis qubit register;
2. a classical record describing the phase correction that must eventually be discharged.
summary: Recycled qubits leave behind a live classical measurement record and an unresolved phase obligation.
title: Memory that remains live

body:
**Answer.** Each shifted controlled addition is replaced by a **controlled add-subtract**. With control bit \(x_k\), it adds \(2^k y\) when \(x_k=1\), but subtracts \(2^k y\) when \(x_k=0\), represented in the enlarged positive-integer register as adding \(2^{n+k}-2^k y\). A controlled add-subtract has the Toffoli cost of an uncontrolled adder: \(n\) with carry-out or \(n-1\) without carry-out. (pp. 1-2, Figs. 1-2.)

For the \(k\)-th multiplication step, the amount added is

\[
(1-x_k)2^{n+k}+(2x_k-1)2^k y.
\]
summary: A controlled add-subtract adds the shifted multiplicand for control 1 and subtracts it for control 0 at the cost of an uncontrolled adder.
title: Replacement for shifted controlled addition

body:
After all \(n\) controlled add-subtract operations, the paper gives the intermediate value

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left((1-x_k)2^{n+k}+(2x_k-1)2^k y\right)
=2xy+2^{2n}-2^n(x+1+y)+y.
\]

The global corrections are:

1. add \(2^n(x+1)\);
2. subtract \(2^{2n}+y\);
3. add \(2^n y\);
4. divide by two by relabeling the qubits.

The reported total for the non-modular, \(2n\)-bit-output schoolbook multiplier is

\[
\boxed{n^2+4n+3\ \text{Toffoli gates}}.
\]

This is compared with \(2n^2+n\) for the controlled-adder construction. (pp. 1-2, Table 1 and Fig. 2.)
summary: The affine intermediate value is globally corrected and shifted to obtain multiplication in \(n^2+4n+3\) Toffolis.
title: Exact intermediate expression and non-modular cost

body:
**Important limitation.** The paper's prime-modulus construction is an **out-of-place Montgomery-representation multiplier**. Its inputs are assumed to be stored in Montgomery form; each `ModMultStep` also contributes garbage, and full cleanup may require copying the result to another register and reversing the multiplier. (pp. 2-4, Fig. 3.)

Therefore it is not a drop-in implementation of an API such as

\[
|a\rangle_{\mathrm{canonical}}\longmapsto |a b\bmod p\rangle_{\mathrm{canonical}}
\]

performed in place. Importing it requires, at minimum, a representation plan for entering and leaving Montgomery form and a decision about the separate result and garbage registers. If the surrounding circuit requires a canonical residue after every operation, conversion and cleanup costs must be included.
summary: The prime multiplier is not a drop-in in-place canonical-field operation because it is out-of-place, Montgomery-form, and garbage-producing.
title: Prime-field interface limitation

body:
The lemma starts with

\[
\sum_x\alpha_x|x\rangle_A|g(x)\rangle_G
\]

and requires a self-adjoint oracle

\[
U_g|x\rangle_A|b\rangle_G
=|x\rangle_A|b\oplus g(x)\rangle_G.
\]

Apply \(H\) to \(G\) and measure \(G\) in the computational basis:

- **Outcome 0, probability \(1/2\):** the register is already uncomputed, leaving
  \[
  \sum_x\alpha_x|x\rangle_A|0\rangle_G.
  \]

- **Outcome 1, probability \(1/2\):** the data register carries the phase
  \[
  \sum_x\alpha_x(-1)^{g(x)}|x\rangle_A|1\rangle_G.
  \]
  The repair applies \(H\) to \(G\), then \(U_g\), then another \(H\) and a NOT on \(G\). Phase kickback cancels \((-1)^{g(x)}\) and resets \(G\) to \(|0\rangle\).

**Repair condition.** The plug-and-play statement depends on \(U_g\) being the self-adjoint XOR oracle above. The expected nonlinear cost is half the cost of invoking that repair oracle, because only the outcome-1 branch uses it. (Lemma 4.1, p. 35.)
summary: Outcome 0 erases the predicate for free; outcome 1 leaves phase kickback and invokes a self-adjoint XOR-oracle repair.
title: The two branches of the one-bit MBU lemma

body:
The reported expected costs are:

| Construction | Expected Toffoli cost | Ancillas |
|---|---:|---:|
| Gidney modular adder | \(\boxed{3.5n}\) | \(2n+3\) |
| Gidney controlled modular adder | \(\boxed{4.5n+0.5}\) | \(2n+3\) |

For the uncontrolled circuit the decomposition is

\[
n+n+n+\frac{n}{2}=3.5n.
\]

For the controlled circuit it is

\[
2n+n+n+\frac{n+1}{2}=4.5n+0.5.
\]

The halved term is the final comparator used to erase the reduction flag. (Theorems 4.4 and 4.9, pp. 36 and 38-39.)
summary: MBU lowers the expected costs to \(3.5n\) and \(4.5n+0.5\) Toffolis for uncontrolled and controlled modular addition.
title: Gidney modular-adder costs after MBU

body:
Only two of the four high-level subroutines need the **external** control \(c\):

1. the first addition, producing \(c x+y\);
2. the final comparison used to uncompute the reduction flag.

The middle comparison against \(p\) is unconditional. The subtraction of \(p\) is controlled by the internally computed comparison/reduction flag, not directly by \(c\). This is why controlling every gate or every modular-adder subroutine would over-control the circuit. (Proposition 3.9, p. 28.)
summary: Only the initial addition and final flag-erasing comparison require the caller’s control.
title: Where the external control is actually required
